source_text: Quod autem filii ex coniugio suscepti naturaliter boni sunt, Apostolo dicente discamus, qui ait de improbis: Relicto naturali usu feminae exarserunt in desideria sua invicem masculi in masculos turpitudinem operantes 70. Ostendit ergo usum feminae et naturalem esse et pro suo modo laudabilem; flagitium autem ex voluntate propria exerceri contra institutionis pudorem. Merito itaque et in bene utentibus genus concupiscentiae modusque laudatur et in turpibus excessus eius punitur. Denique eodem tempore Deus Abrahae et Sarrae marcentia aevo membra vegetavit, quo in Sodomis ipsa igneo imbre punivit 71. Si igitur putas accusandum membrorum vigorem, quoniam per ipsum Sodomitae flagitiis obliti sunt, accusabis etiam creaturam panis et vini, quoniam hinc quoque eos peccasse Scriptura divina significavit; dicit enim Dominus per Ezechielem prophetam: Verumtamen hae iniquitates Sodomae sororis tuae superbia; in saturitate panum et abundantia vini fluebant ipsa et filii eius, et manum pauperis et egentis non adiuvabant 72. Elige iam utrum mavis: aut reputa divino operi commixtionem corporum aut creaturam panis et vini similiter malam esse defini. Quod si feceris, aperte Manichaeus esse convinceris. Concupiscentiae autem naturalis qui modum tenet, bono bene utitur; qui modum non tenet, bono male utitur. Quid dicis ergo
pass_a_gloss: Let us learn from the Apostle that sons taken from marriage are good by nature, who says of the wicked: Having left the natural use of the female they burned toward their desires for one another, males working shamefulness toward males. He therefore shows that the use of the female is both natural and praiseworthy according to its own measure; but a shameful deed is exercised from one's own will against the modesty of the institution. Rightly therefore both in those using well the kind and measure of desire is praised, and in the shameful its excess is punished. Finally at the same time God made vigorous Abraham's and Sarah's members withering with age, with which in Sodom he punished those very ones with a fiery rain. If therefore you think the vigor of the members must be accused, since through it the Sodomites were covered in shameful deeds, you will also accuse the creature of bread and wine, since divine Scripture signified that they sinned from this too. Choose now which you prefer: either count the mixing of bodies as a divine work, or likewise define the creature of bread and wine as evil. He who holds the measure of natural desire uses a good well; he who does not hold the measure uses a good badly. Why then do you say that the good of marriages cannot be accused by the original evil which is drawn from there, as the evil of adulteries cannot be excused by the natural good which is born from there?

pass_b_english: Let us learn from the apostle that children born from marriage are good by nature. Speaking of the ungodly, he says: “Abandoning the natural use of the woman, they burned with desire for one another, males doing what is shameful with males” (Romans 1:27). He therefore shows that the use of the woman is natural and, within its proper bounds, praiseworthy; shameful conduct, however, is committed by a person’s own will against the modesty of the created order. So the kind of desire and its proper measure are rightly praised in those who use it well, while its excess is punished in those who act shamefully.

Indeed, at the same time that God revived Abraham’s and Sarah’s bodily organs, withered by age, he punished those same organs at Sodom with a rain of fire (Genesis 18:10–14; 19:24). If, then, you think the vigor of the organs must be condemned because through it the Sodomites became covered in shameful deeds, you will also condemn bread and wine as created things, since divine Scripture indicates that these too were means of their sin. For the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel: “These, indeed, were the wrongs of your sister Sodom: pride; she and her children overflowed with an abundance of bread and wine, and they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). Now choose whichever you prefer: either count the bodily union as God’s work, or likewise declare bread and wine evil as created things. If you do that, you will plainly be proved a Manichaean.

Anyone who keeps natural desire within bounds uses a good thing well; anyone who fails to keep it within bounds uses a good thing badly. Why, then, do you say: “The good of marriage cannot be condemned because of the original evil derived from it, just as the evil of adultery cannot be excused by the natural good born from it”? With these words you have granted what you denied and taken away what you granted. Nothing occupies you more than making yourself hard to understand.

Show bodily marriage without sexual union, or give this activity a single name and call marriage either good or evil. You certainly promised to define marriage as good. If marriage is good, if the human being who is the fruit of marriage is good, and if this fruit, God’s work, cannot be evil when born through good from good, where, then, is the original evil that so many prior findings have ruled out?

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
